nameStory: Bearberry gets its name from the Latin 'uva-ursi,' which literally means 'grape of the bear' — bears apparently love munching on these bright red berries! The scientific name Arctostaphylos also means 'bear grapes' in Greek, so this little plant is doubly dedicated to our furry friends. Indigenous peoples called it kinnikinnick, meaning 'smoking mixture,' because the leaves were traditionally used in tobacco blends.
description: Bearberry is a low-growing, mat-forming shrub that hugs the ground like a living carpet. This tough little evergreen rarely grows taller than a foot, instead spreading outward to form dense patches. Its small, leathery leaves stay green year-round, and in late spring it produces tiny bell-shaped flowers that look like miniature lanterns. By late summer, bright red berries appear that practically glow against the dark green foliage.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, ground-hugging mats that spread horizontally rather than growing tall, creating natural carpets across the landscape

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves feel thick and leathery to the touch, with smooth edges and a waxy surface that stays bright green all winter

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about the size of small peas that feel mealy and dry when squeezed, persisting well into fall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to pink bell-shaped flowers that hang like little lanterns, feeling papery and delicate when gently touched

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Reddish-brown stems that feel smooth when young but develop a slightly shreddy texture as they age and trail along the ground

habitat: Bearberry thrives in poor, sandy, or rocky soils where other plants struggle, often carpeting coastal dunes, mountain slopes, and exposed ridges. In New England, look for it in pine barrens, along rocky shorelines, and on windswept mountain summits where the soil is acidic and well-drained. It's particularly common in areas with harsh conditions — think places that get blasted by salt spray or mountain winds.

seasonality.spring: Tiny bell-shaped white to pink flowers appear in late spring, clustering at branch tips and giving off a subtle sweet fragrance when you get close.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and small green berries begin forming while the evergreen leaves maintain their glossy, dark green color throughout the heat.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and become the plant's most obvious feature, glowing like tiny Christmas ornaments against the persistent green foliage.
seasonality.winter: Remains easily identifiable by its evergreen mat-forming habit and any remaining red berries, often partially buried under snow but still visible.

funFact: Bearberry leaves contain so many tannins that they were once used to tan leather — the same compounds that make the leaves feel so thick and leathery also made them valuable to early leather workers!
confusionNotes: Bearberry's low, mat-forming growth makes it fairly distinctive, but it might be confused with wintergreen, which also has evergreen leaves and red berries. Remember: wintergreen has minty-scented leaves when crushed and grows more upright, while bearberry forms ground-hugging carpets and has no scent.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bearberry,' the berries are technically edible for humans but are quite dry and mealy — they're much better appreciated for their beauty than their flavor. The plant is incredibly hardy and long-lived, with some patches potentially surviving for decades in harsh mountain and coastal environments.
compareHints: Bearberry is the only Arctostaphylos species you'll find in New England, but within the heath family, it's distinguished from other low-growing members like wintergreen by its complete lack of scent when crushed and its distinctive mat-forming habit. Unlike cranberries (also in the heath family), bearberry leaves are much thicker and more leathery, and the plant doesn't require bog conditions.
